_comment: One contract, one file. The backend decides how long a subprocess may run; the n8n node
decides how long to wait for the answer. Those were once written independently and given
the SAME number, which reads as agreement and is in fact a guaranteed loss for the caller:
n8n starts its clock when the request arrives, the route sets the stage and only then
spawns the child, so the client always reaches its deadline first. It abandons the request
while the backend is still killing the process group and composing a reply.
Nothing errored. A live run sat in `improving_mutation / running tests (full suite)` for
6h47m with the dashboard showing it in progress, and 312 of 457 units were never attempted.
The backend is Java and the workflow generator is JavaScript, so neither can require the
other's module. Re-typing these numbers in two languages is exactly the defect above.
They live here, and both sides read this file.
ceilingMs is a SUM over a route's child processes, not a per-call limit — reading it as
per-call is how /api/coverage/run came to allow half of what it needs. A Java test asserts
each ceiling still equals the composition of perCallMs described in `composedOf`.

/api/coverage/run.why: the project's own JaCoCo, then a full retry with our agent when that produces no report because its agent sits in an inactive profile — two sequential builds, not one

/api/pit/run.why: test-compile and then PIT. The compile is not optional: `mvn <plugin>:<goal>` runs no lifecycle phase, so without it PIT finds no classes and reports a score of zero

_httpMarginWhy: How much longer the caller waits than the work can take. Not a rounding allowance: when a run does hit its ceiling the backend still has to kill a process group — Maven and Gradle fork Surefire and PIT minion JVMs — drain what they wrote, parse a report and serialise a reply. Five minutes is generous on purpose; the cost of being too generous is noticing a dead run late, and the cost of being too tight is the defect above.
